data.title: How bank compliance leaders are engaging with regulators
data.description:
• Key insight: Banks are facing the challenge, and opportunity, to rework their compliance protocols as regulators are enacting broad changes to bank reporting requirements.
  • Expert quote: "A strong foundation will enable you to ensure that you are complying with consumer compliance no matter what the environment is." — Citi CCO Jennifer Taylor

As federal regulatory agencies are defining market structures in areas such as stablecoin regulation and enacting sweeping changes in bank regulation on multiple fronts, some bank compliance leaders are actively adjusting their risk management strategies.

"It's certainly an exciting time to be in banking, especially in risk management and compliance," U.S. Bank Chief Risk Officer Jodi Richard said during a panel at American Banker's Most Powerful Women In Banking Conference on Wednesday.

Nicole Anderson, principal for FS regulatory advisory services at PwC, cautioned that agencies facing staffing cuts will be relying more heavily on banks to do the legwork of risk management.

"Regulators are already telling us, 'We don't have enough resources to come in and do the same things we used to do. If you can't show us that you really have identified the risk, understand the risk and have identified appropriate controls or control gaps, you're next in line for the criticism.' We were starting to see that a little before the [regulatory] shift, but this is now going to magnify that. It's a really good time to start thinking about the fundamentals of your risk management."

Kara West, chief enterprise risk officer for Capital One, said that banks have a unique opportunity in the current regulatory environment to "push back" and engage with regulators in new ways.

"To be honest, it's a pretty tough time for them – I'd hate to be a regulator right now," she said. "We are working with our regulators to think about where we can bring them along on the changes we're making. We feel way more openness than what we've seen before, and we're trying to take advantage of that and build relationships."

Richard said that there are also new opportunities for banks to customize and adjust their risk management approaches.

"It is a great time to be a risk manager," she said. "It puts you back in the driver's seat to make sure that you're allocating resources to the highest-level emerging risk where you actually feel there is exposure, driving that a little bit more than following things that might be more interesting to a wide set of banks but not as applicable to you."

Read more:

  • OCC leaves room for stablecoin yield maneuvers in final rule
  • 'A team sport:' Responding to cyber threats in the age of AI
  • BlackRock's Mullin on a culture of 'maximum flexibility'
  • 'We could lose our edge': Bankers on competing for digital assets

Even as compliance departments are re-prioritizing their risk focuses and incorporating new tools, such as AI, Citi Chief Compliance Officer for Banking and International Jennifer Taylor said that sticking to the fundamentals of risk management will help institutions. 

"A strong foundation will enable you to ensure that you are complying with consumer compliance no matter what the environment is," she said. "This more targeted focus of risk enables us to be a bit more forward-looking and to watch out for emerging risks, which is an important way to manage risk for this fast-moving environment."

Taylor noted that much of her bank's risk management had previously revolved around risks that had happened before, but she is working to challenge some of those assumptions.

"Some of the compliance reporting metrics were created because of the situation before and that metric continued to appear in compliance reporting for years after the metric wasn't delivering any value," she said. "Now, we constantly challenge ourselves on, 'What's the purpose?' Maturing will help us continue to manage risk appropriately from a safety and soundness perspective, no matter where we manage it."

data.title: Independents lag on AI. Here's how they can catch up
data.description:
• Key insight: In the employee advisors vs. independent advisors and AI race, employee advisors remain the winners, but as structural efforts improve, independent advisors can gain ground.
  • What's at stake: proper access to the right tools means independent advisors can enjoy the same benefits as their larger counterparts.
  • Forward look: Independents doubled their use of AI in a year according to JD Power

Financial advisors who use AI have reported being more satisfied in their jobs, but the happiness is not spread evenly. Nearly three-quarters of employee advisors [employed by large firms] actively use AI, but only 42% of independent advisors do the same.

While in theory the tools are available to everyone, larger firms are better equipped to roll out AI to employees, meaning that smaller and independent firms need to accelerate their governance procedures, vetting processes and training to catch up.

The AI gap between large and small wealth firms

The gap isn't due to a lack of access to technology across the industry. Smaller firms are taking big steps, according to the JD Power study that measured advisor satisfaction and AI usage. The number of independent advisors who reported using AI jumped from 19% to 42 % in just one year, according to that study.

Rather, it all comes down to structure.

Wirehouses "have the ability to really build out this technology, integrate it into their platform, establish the rules and train the advisors," said Joe McQuaid, COO of Tampa, Florida-based Concurrent Investment Advisors, in an interview. 

James Spinelli, founder and CEO of Great Valley Advisor Group in Berwyn, Pennsylvania, grew his firm from a couple of advisors over 12 years ago to a 215-advisor firm that now manages just under $15 billion. He also developed a compensation tool called Advisor BB (Advisor Book of Business) that he deployed to about 80 RIAs before selling this past year to Bozeman, Montana-based AdvicePay. 

In the case of RIAs versus wirehouses, it is a matter of dollars and cents, he said. Bigger firms also have "the governance and they've got everything in place for that tool that they want to roll out," he said. 

For firms that want an overhaul, Spinelli believes deployment has to be strategic. 

"If I rolled out a CRM and was like 'everybody has to use Wealthbox, there's no Salesforce [or] Redtail,'" he said, adoption would rise faster, "but that's not necessarily a good thing because you take away choice [and] flexibility."

Addressing the cost and integration factors

One challenge smaller firms grapple with around AI is cost. Basic systems that meet the criteria advisors need, including proper safekeeping of client information, can run into the thousands of dollars per month. 

Dan Eyre is COO of the software company DeepVest, which recently launched Day One. Day One is the company's answer to the financial dilemma that offers smaller firms a suite of its AI tools and solutions for a low-entry price point for the first year. 

"If they have the time and the tools, they're able to better serve a client than a larger firm, where they don't get quite as much mind share from the advisor or the wealth team," he said. 

By targeting smaller firms, Eyre said, the services are a win-win for both DeepVest and its clients. 

"We know they're going to win that business," Eyre said. "They're going to use those tools and put them to better use because they don't have all the red tape."

One potential pitfall firms face without a streamlined system, according to McQuaid, is integration. Firms might not want to invest in an entire suite and opt to instead take what is known as the "bolt-on" route. When firms choose to bolt-on by adding AI features to their existing legacy software, the integration problem surfaces. 

"If AI is added to every one of the tools that we use, it still doesn't solve the problem," said McQuaid. "In the independent world… one of the issues with using all of this different fintech is [it] doesn't integrate well. The data doesn't flow back and forth between one system and another system."

For instance, an advisor using a financial planning tool and CRM that are not fully integrated with one another requires duplicate data. "If you have an integrated layer that's on top of your system that's utilizing AI, I think the experience is going to be far superior," said McQuaid.

Governance as the unlock

As governance catches up, Spinelli expects AI adoption will "skyrocket," with independents eventually surpassing their larger firm counterparts. Firms without clear governance policies risk having their advisors "skating on this fine line," he said, "of, 'oh, can I put a client's name in here? And is that going to be an issue with this tool that we're using?'"

Getting ahead on policies includes clarity around what governance should cover. 

"I think governance is extremely critical, and making sure that you have governance in place," said McQuaid, adding that governance can outline which AI tools firms use and the data they allow those tools to employ. 

"If you're not using an enterprise model, I would never put personal identifiable information (PII) in any AI model," he said. "Those governance rules are important." 

Larger firms, McQuaid said, can fold strong governance and compliance policies directly into operations. 

"Independent firms, I believe, have a lot of work that needs to be done ahead of time," he said.

Other governance measures could include:

  • Running AI tools through vendor due diligence, similarly to the process used with CRM or planning tools.
  • Asking the vendor if it trains its models on the firm's data.
  • Checking the vendor's history with client data, including around breaches or data leaks.
  • Limiting data exposure with new vendors that lack a track record rather than ruling them out.

For firms that don't have it in their budget to deploy an entire AI infrastructure from scratch, McQuaid suggests buying off-the-shelf tools as a more realistic approach. 

"The barrier of entry into building out an AI infrastructure is not low," he said. "It's a high barrier."

That barrier is why he believes more firms will move toward what he referred to as "consumption versus moving towards creation."

Another way to thoughtfully choose tools to deploy comes courtesy of firmwide pain points. A simple review of where the issues lie can result in a better understanding of the collective issues an AI tool could solve. 

"Build a plan around solving that pain," said McQuaid. "Then you can choose the tool that fits your platform."

Once tools are in place, McQuaid suggests tracking and measuring results. 

"What I found with a lot of smaller independent advisors is they're actually spending more time on the technology. So instead of it actually doing what it's supposed to do … they're spending less time with their clients and more time on the AI."

data.title: BankThink Stablecoins are essential to the health of the federal balance sheet
data.description:
• Key insight: Stablecoin issuers back their dollar-pegged assets with short-dated U.S. Treasuries. As the industry expands, they are picking up the slack left by traditional buyers who have soured on U.S. government debt.
  • Supporting data: Data from the Fed's research shows stablecoin issuers hold roughly $200 billion in U.S. Treasuries, with Tether accounting for $141 billion of the figure.

A declining global appetite for U.S. Treasuries has been in the spotlight, with Japan, China and France leading the pack as sellers. Analysts cite inflation concerns, Trump tariffs, lack of fiscal restraint, and an escalating global bond sell-off as factors behind the pivot away from Treasuries, but data also suggests private investors and stablecoin issuers have emerged as new sources of demand, and may play a role in bolstering the U.S. dollar.

According to the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, rising stablecoin issuer demand for short-dated Treasuries is reducing the impact of foreign governments selling U.S. Treasuries.

Data from the Fed's research shows stablecoin issuers hold roughly $200 billion in U.S. Treasuries, with Tether (USDT issuer) accounting for $141 billion of the figure. This puts Tether ahead of several U.S. allies who were traditionally large buyers.

The Fed further estimates that if the current demand trend sustains alongside stablecoin market cap expansion, stablecoin issuers' ownership of short-duration U.S. Treasuries could reach $400 billion by 2030. Standard Chartered, meanwhile, projects the stablecoin market capitalization to surpass $2 trillion by 2028; if it hits that milestone, short-dated Treasury bill demand could rise to $1 trillion. This level of increasing and consistent demand for U.S. Treasuries provides a stabilizing force, protecting USD's status as the world's reserve currency, and, therefore, U.S. interest rates and related markets like real estate. With more than $30 trillion in debt, the U.S. borrows $10 billion net every business day. It's not ideal from a geopolitics standpoint to be reliant on global powers like China to continue to purchase U.S. debt. The increased purchasing power of stablecoin issues helps to even-out that power dynamic. 

Demand for stablecoins and the resulting impact on Treasury markets has been driven by financial institutions and financial technology companies pushing to tokenize assets by bringing them on-chain. Self-published data from Visa highlighted exponential growth in its stablecoin card programs, with more than 160 active worldwide and payment volume up 200% year over year. Circle's Payments Network currently has 175 financial institutions enrolled, and the recently launched Arc Level 1 live blockchain network includes the Intercontinental Exchange, Mastercard, Visa, Standard Chartered, and BlackRock among its validator members. 

These figures highlight the critical role stablecoins play in transfers, foreign exchange, payments, and lending, including real-world asset tokenization where stocks, commodities, Treasuries, and more are being brought on-chain for 24/7 trading in crypto markets and soon on Wall Street. 

Due to their forays into tokenized assets, fintech and TradFi companies are accelerating stablecoin adoption and contributing to their growing impact on the U.S. economy. 

Read more:

  • OCC leaves room for stablecoin yield maneuvers in final rule
  • 'We could lose our edge': Bankers on competing for digital assets
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026
  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions

Treasury demand is central to the stablecoin flywheel because on-chain settlement requires a dollar that essentially "lives" online, and each dollar minted by a regulated issuer is backed by a short-dated Treasury or repo position.
The recently passed GENIUS Act also requires that issuers back every token 1:1 and limits reserves to cash, deposits or Treasuries dated less than 93 days. 

With the total stablecoin market cap sitting at $305 billion and the two largest issuers (Tether (USDT) and Circle (USDC) holding approximately $220 billion in Treasury-linked reserves, this figure, and its impact on U.S. Treasury markets, is expected to grow as stablecoin volumes expand with institutional finance initiatives related to asset tokenization.

The trajectory of the circulating supply of tokenized equities has skyrocketed since the Sept. 15 failed procedural cloture vote for the CLARITY Act in the U.S. Senate. After the failed vote, the CFTC and SEC stepped in, announcing several rules that let stablecoin and RWA issuers get busy. The writing is no longer "on the wall." The mass adoption and integration of stablecoins to the U.S. and global economy is happening as we speak. 

The accelerating pace at which tokenized assets are being brought on-chain, and stablecoins' role in these processes, validate the view that stablecoins are essential to the growth of the U.S. economy and future of capital formation across global markets.

data.title: How scrutiny of private-credit valuations will impact banks
data.description:
• Key insight: The SEC and state insurance regulators are trying to ensure that the valuations of opaque, illiquid private-credit loans are accurate. Changes in how those investments are valued could have knock-on effects for banks. 
  • What's at stake: The links between private credit, life-insurance companies and banks could contribute to systemic instability, experts warn.

Private-credit valuations are coming under increased scrutiny from federal and state regulators, setting off alarm bells about banks' growing exposure to hard-to-value, illiquid private assets.

Private-credit assets typically are illiquid, individually negotiated loans that don't trade on any secondary market. Because the assets cannot be priced, they have historically been offered only to accredited investors. 

But Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Paul Atkins is seeking to expand access to individual investors. Last month, the SEC put asset managers on notice to "maintain vigor" around valuations. The reminder came on the heels of explosive growth in private credit.  Specifically within registered funds, private credit surged to $270 billion in 2025, a 60% jump from $170 billion in 2020, the SEC said.

"The growing accessibility of private assets, including private credit, calls for a critical reminder that registrants maintain rigor over how these assets are valued and how those valuations and asset risk characteristics are disclosed to investors," SEC Chief Accountant Kurt Hohl wrote in a joint statement with Brian Daly, director of the SEC's division of investment management. 

Some of the banking industry's exposure to private credit is through life insurers. Life insurers an estimated $1 trillion invested in private credit, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners, a trade group representing state regulators, pegged insurers' exposure at $1.21 trillion as of the end of 2025. Banks have significant counterparty exposure to life insurers.

Life-insurance companies are among the major firms financing the AI data center buildout, with significant exposure to AI-linked debt. If AI-linked loans default or lose value, losses could spread through the financial system, increasing the risk of contagion to banks, some experts warn. 

Historically, life insurers have relied on safe assets like Treasuries and high-grade corporate bonds to meet future policyholder obligations. But private-equity firms have taken over numerous life insurers, and they sought higher returns in low interest-rate environments by investing heavily in private credit and loans to affiliated companies. 

What's more, banks' ties to the private-credit market could deepen as a result of several proposed changes to bank capital rules. Lower risk weights could make it more attractive for banks to finance or hold certain private credit-related assets.

The shift toward illiquid, but potentially higher-yielding private loans has sparked ramped-up scrutiny. 

"It's important to understand how important valuation is to the SEC," said John Mahon, a partner at the law firm Cleary Gottlieb. "Investors have to have confidence in the valuation process because you need robust valuation in order to get comfortable with the expansion of retail products." 

Nadja Dreff, senior vice president and sector lead for global insurance and pension ratings at Morningstar DBRS, said not every insurer is suited to holding illiquid, opaque investments. 

"We haven't gone through a full credit cycle so we don't know how these investments will perform," Dreff said. "The complexity also varies. There are structures that are quite complex and not easily understood." 

Importantly, the SEC's statement is part of a proposal that would allow registered investment advisers to charge performance fees to a broader range of investors, mutual funds and exchange traded funds, in the push to expand individual investors' access to private markets. 

Whenever there are performance-based fees involved, Mahon said, "you have to have confidence in valuations because now the fund managers are being paid even more concretely on those valuations."

Dreff said there is a potential conflict of interest when private-equity owners receive fees from insurers they own. Morningstar DBRS analysts are assessing whether asset managers' parent companies have "undue influence," and whether insurance companies are making independent investment decisions, she said.

"There could be a mismatch in the relationship where the asset manager or private-equity owner also receives fees from the insurer that it owns," Dreff said. "The more investments that the private-equity owner could offer up and provide, that the insurer accepts as appropriate and buys into their portfolio, the higher the fees that the parent or the private-equity owner earns."

Banks' exposure to private credit

Banks' counterparty exposure to life insurers comes through credit lines, funding agreement notes, derivative contracts and syndicated private loans, experts said. If an insurer experiences a run or regulatory seizure, banks could face collateral haircuts and broader systemic instability, experts said.

Though statutory accounting rules require very high reserves for certain products like term life insurance and universal life insurance, many insurers routinely cede liabilities and transfer a portion of their risk to reinsurers, which reduces the amount of statutory reserves they are required to hold on their balance sheets.

Mayra Rodriguez Valladares, a risk consultant and managing principal at MRV Associates, said state regulators are also pushing insurance companies to be more forthcoming about their risk exposures. 

"Private-equity firms are sitting on a lot of assets that they haven't been able to sell," said Valladares, who trains bankers and regulators about risks they are exposed to. "State regulators are looking under the hood of these life-insurance companies. It's very opaque to the people to whom it should be transparent." 

Tom Gober, a forensic accounting and expert witness, claims that major insurance carriers are holding tens of billions in short-term funding agreements while carrying razor-thin cash reserves meant to cover policyholders' future payouts. He has alleged that some insurance companies have been masking their true financial health through offshore reinsurance and affiliated investments.

"Everyone is starting to talk about how this is not the insurance industry we used to know," said Gober. "It's a high-risk, dangerous, illiquid industry."

A core reason for the higher risk is that private-equity firms and asset managers have bought life insurers and increasingly have invested in affiliated businesses. Last year, there were 139 life insurers with a combined $321 billion of affiliated investment assets, according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.

The NAIC, which creates model laws and accounting rules, has developed several proposals aimed at getting a grasp of life insurers' valuations of private credit — in part because current reporting requirements vary substantially.

The NAIC is conducting a 2026 year-end review to address the adequacy of life-insurer reserves, also with a focus on valuations. The review seeks to connect the quality of asset valuations to the assumptions used to demonstrate that adequate reserves have been set aside for policyholders.

In 2025, life insurers' exposure to private-credit funds, privately rated bonds and business development companies totaled $544 billion, the NAIC has found. 

A key issue cited by both the SEC and the NAIC involves so-called Level 3 assets, whose fair value cannot be determined by market pricing and is based on what the industry calls "unobservable inputs." The NAIC also is considering whether operating subsidiaries and difficult-to-value private structures need different treatment.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • BMO's top US executive to depart in leadership shuffle

Dreff said Morningstar DBRS analysts currently are assessing the quality of individual insurers' risk-management frameworks and overall governance.

"Once we get comfort around that, it gives us an added sort of confidence that an insurer has the appropriate structures and guardrails in place to protect policyholders," she said. 

As for the SEC, it has said the need for accurate valuations applies to all private funds. The agency has cautioned firms against using boilerplate language or ignoring current market conditions when evaluating assets.

"The whole system is stable only if insurance companies have illiquid liabilities to match their illiquid private-credit investments," said Dreff.

data.title: Looking ahead, Huntington sees growth, warnings signs
data.description:
• Key insight: Huntington remains excited about the opportunities its new markets and national lending verticals present, but CEO Steven Steinour says high levels of market turbulence are a cause for concern. 
  • Supporting data: The company projects earnings of between $1.75 to 1.83 per share in 2027.

Though some of Huntington Bancshares' business lines struggled in the third quarter, commercial-and-industrial lending hit on all cylinders.

The Columbus, Ohio-based company's C&I balances grew 3% to $94 billion during the three months ended Sept. 30, helping to offset declines in its commercial real estate, residential mortgage and auto-loan portfolios.

"The environment for commercial customers is still constructive," Brant Standridge, Huntington's president, said Thursday on a call with analysts. "We're still seeing customers pursue growth opportunities. We're still seeing customers execute on a number of strategic initiatives, and I would say [capital expenditure] is still very strong."

The C&I expansion reflects progress in the $287.8 billion-asset Huntington's strategy of adding national commercial-lending verticals, according to executives at the bank.

It's launched 14 verticals since 2015, including one hatched in August that focuses on serving community and property associations and their management partners. Earlier this month, Huntington unveiled an international corporate banking group to work with multinational companies entering or expanding in the U.S.

"That group of corporate and specialty businesses generated $11 billion of loan growth in the last year. That is still in the very early stages," Standridge told American Banker on Thursday.

Headwinds outside of C&I

Outside the C&I arena, Huntington's loan-growth efforts produced more mixed results. There were small gains in home-equity and marine and recreational vehicle lending, but balances in the CRE, home mortgage and automobile portfolios declined by a combined $872 million from June 30, 2026, levels.

The CRE issues stemmed from a surge in construction-loan paydowns in July and August. Huntington slowed auto and mortgage production on its own due to pricing concerns.

"We're seeing areas where we're just not getting risk-adjusted returns," Chairman and CEO Steve Steinour said on the conference call. "We'd rather return capital to shareholders than put it out at what we think would be very low returns, in some cases not even meeting our minimum expectations."

The third quarter was Huntington's first full three-month stretch since converting former Cadence Bancorp customers to its operating system in June. In January, it converted former Veritex Holdings clients.

Acquiring Houston-based Cadence and Dallas-based Veritex added more than $60 billion of assets and expanded Huntington's footprint in Texas and the Southeast.

Commenting on the conference call, Standridge said Huntington has had good success in retaining bankers and clients from Veritex and Cadence, and believes its prospects for growing revenue in the new markets are better than previously expected.

"We're feeling positive about where we are and very optimistic about the opportunities that these markets present for the company," Standridge said.

Huntington reported third-quarter net income totaling $680 million, roughly level with its $686 million second-quarter profit. Year-over-year comparisons were skewed by the additions of Cadence and Veritex.

The third-quarter result amounted to $0.33 per share. Excluding merger-related expenses, Huntington's adjusted earnings-per-share totaled $0.38, topping the consensus estimate of $0.35, according to S&P Capital IQ.

Huntington reported deposits totaling $224.7 billion on Sept. 30, up 1% on a quarter-over-quarter basis. Loans of $191.4 billion were also up 1%.

Read more:

  • Inside Fifth Third's 'innovation economy' ambitions
  • Citi hires Google's director of engineering, shuffles AI leaders
  • Wells Fargo prevails in pay fight with former CEO Tim Sloan
  • Bank OZK, heavy in CRE loans, makes progress in diversifying

Jefferies analyst David Chiaverini characterized Huntington's results as "mixed." In a research note, he said earnings per share were higher than expected, but he also pointed to the muted loan growth.

Huntington, which has reported earnings totaling $0.91 per share through the first nine months of 2026, is projecting earnings per share of $1.75 to $1.83 in 2027. The company believes it will achieve a return on tangible common equity of 17% to 18%, above the 14.6% reported for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

At the same time, Steinour said uncertainty surrounding the ultimate impact of tariffs, interest-rate hikes and inflation means Huntington will tread carefully.

"Having been around this for four-and-one-half decades, I'm a little more cautious, perhaps, than some of my peers," Steinour said. "There's just so much volatility in the markets today. I don't recall the amount of challenges that we're seeing globally at any time in my career. We're going to be sensitive to that in terms of how much volume we want to add."

data.title: Bread: Inflation making spending 'increasingly selective'
data.description:
• Key insights: While credit sales grew 9% in the third quarter, Bread Financial CEO Ralph Andretta said that consumers with lower credit scores showed greater selectivity in their purchasing patterns.
  • What's at stake: Persistent inflation and high gas prices are starting to change consumers' purchasing patterns, but have yet to impact overall spending or repayment rates. 

Persistent inflation and high gas prices have yet to impact consumer spending or repayment rates, according to Bread Financial, but some consumers are being more cautious. 

Bread Financial CEO Ralph Andretta said on the company's third quarter earnings call Thursday that consumer behavior continued to remain resilient, but that spending "was increasingly intentional. 

"Higher credit quality cardholders remained a consistent source of strength, while consumers with lower credit risk scores showed greater selectivity in their purchasing patterns," Andretta said. 

Bread's credit sales increased 9% year over year to $7.4 billion as consumers with higher credit scores continued to spend and consumers with lower credit scores adapted to the higher cost of fuel by shopping for deals and pulling back on some discretionary spending, such as dining out at restaurants.

"Consumers are obviously spending more on fuel, and we're seeing restaurant spending come down," Chief Financial Officer Perry Beberman told American Banker in an interview following the company's earnings call. "Fast casual, no change, but full-service restaurant spend is lower. Similarly, we're seeing lower [travel and entertainment] costs, which means customers are making choices to make sure they're still able to meet their needs within their budget." 

That doesn't mean consumers aren't traveling, Beberman said. "We actually have the same number of hotel stays, but the average transactions are down. Middle America is seeking deals on hotel stays or trading down from a higher end hotel to more value-priced hotels." 

Consumers were staying current on their bills, too. Bread's delinquency rate decreased 47 basis points year over year to 5.57%, and its net loss rate dropped 99 basis points to 6.4%. 

Looking to the fourth quarter, Beberman said he expects holiday spending to be delayed this year due to the election in November. 

"Anytime you're in a period like this where you've got an election right in the middle of it, retailers are usually hold back on their advertising and their deals because everyone's mailbox is getting filled up with political campaign ads," Beberman said. 

Still, Bread is expecting a "pretty strong" holiday shopping season, Beberman said. 

"Higher end consumers are going to spend and spend well," he said. "Middle income folks are going to continue to spend for their kids and families and friends and go out and do things. They're just going to be a little more value conscious." 

Broadly, Bread posted a "solid quarter" that sets the company up to finish off the year strong, according to Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Sanjay Sakhrani. "We left earnings with more conviction in the fundamentals and our estimates next year," he said. Revenue was up 5% year over year to $1 billion, while end-of-period loans increased 7% to $18.9 billion. And net interest margin came in at 18.89%, an increase of 40 basis points from the second quarter and 8 basis points from a year ago.

data.title: Visa, Mastercard bet on AI, crypto ahead of earnings
data.description:
• Key insight: Visa and Mastercard both released several AI and blockchain-related products in recent days. 
  • What's at stake: The credit card companies announce third quarter earnings next week, and investors will be looking at revenue sources such as value-added non-payment services. 

With card-issuing banks pressured to build strategies for agentic commerce and digital assets, Visa and Mastercard are expanding their abilities to sell into these trends. 

Both card brands have released services in the past few days, and in the case of Visa, there were rumors of a potential $2.5 billion deal to acquire cryptocurrency technology firm Fireblocks. Visa said it does not comment on rumors or speculation, while Fireblocks did not return a request for comment (Fireblocks denied Visa talks in crypto site Coindesk.)

Supplier payments

Even before talk of a Fireblocks acquisition, Visa recently released several tools designed for agentic commerce and digital assets. Earlier this week, the card company introduced services for corporate payments, including new analytics for supplier spending, virtual-card fraud prevention, and a live pilot enabling trusted AI agents to complete B2B invoice payments."The B2B world is filled with very routine manual processes that are just begging for automation," Darren Parslow, global head of Visa Commercial Solutions, told American Banker. 

The new analytics, called SESA 2.0, use AI to produce spend analysis and to help businesses identify high-potential supplier opportunities. Another product, Visa Commercial Fraud Solutions, helps issuers and businesses validate suppliers, authenticate virtual-card payment activity and apply controls before a payment is approved."What we're really trying to do is build the ecosystem for agentic commerce," Parslow said.

An additional initiative, a pilot with Billtrust, enables trusted AI agents to initiate and help complete approved invoice payments through supplier portals, using Visa Intelligent Commerce and Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol.

"What's great about this pilot is it addresses both sides, the buyers and suppliers, for a fully automated payment from invoice approval to supplier acceptance," Parslow said. 

On the digital asset front, Visa this week took its Visa Direct stablecoin project out of pilot testing. In the initial deployment, Inyo Global, a Visa Direct processor that has banks, fintechs and payment companies among its clients, is supporting stablecoin processing for Visa Direct clients and partners. These businesses will have the option to  prefund cross-border payouts through Visa Direct with USDC in near real time, rather than relying solely on traditional funding windows.

"The next chapter for stablecoins is adoption," said Vira Platonova, global head of Visa Direct. In a release. 

Visa's digital asset strategy could get a boost if it were to acquire Fireblocks, which sells institutional custody, stablecoin settlement and tokenization, among other services. Visa and Mastercard have both made stablecoin support a key pillar of their value-added services strategies–or their quest to draw revenue from sources beyond card payments. 

Fruit from Mastercard's BVNK deal

Mastercard's moves over the past week include launching Global Money Platform with BVNK, with Nuvei, Marqeta, Ontop and Beem among the first users. The platform enables banks, fintechs and businesses to use software or an application programming interface to support traditional currency and stablecoins. Mastercard Move supports local bank payouts, with more than 40 currencies planned to be available by 2017.

Mastercard closed a $1.8 billion deal to acquire digital asset technology firm BVNK in August, supplying Mastercard with tools to scale digital assets–a goal Visa could also address if it acquired Fireblocks. 

"Stablecoins used to be just about powering crypto trading. It's now becoming a payment instrument and a way to store value as well," Raj Dhamodharan, executive vice president of blockchain and digital asset products at Mastercard, told American Banker. 

Mastercard in recent days also launched Stablecoin Security, a product designed to assess fraud and other criminal risk before funds move from traditional rails to blockchain, and a demonstration of Agent Pay for Machines. This product enables AI agents to autonomously locate and pay for digital services based on rules set by humans. The move to agentic commerce builds on top of earlier moves the card network made to prepare for AI payments, including agentic AI protocols.

"With a lot of agentic commerce options, you can use these cards on the street today, they can be paired with a trusted agent," Dhamodharan said. 

Courting investors

Visa reports earrings on Tuesday after the market closes, while Mastercard reports Thursday before the opening. 

Mastercard's stock is up about 11% since late October 2025; while Visa's stock is up about 20%. Mastercard's most recent earnings report beat analysts' expectations, as did Visa's earnings. 

 In a research note, KeyBanc Capital Markets notes that Visa and Mastercard's work in agentic commerce positions the card networks well to offer services within guidance for agentic commerce that a group of large banks issued earlier this year.
